text: Train the same model architecture twice, even on the same data, and you can get two different results — a different random seed, an unrecorded hyperparameter tweak, a dependency bump nobody wrote down. Without a system that captures exactly what produced a given model, reproducing a result becomes a guessing game. That's the problem experiment tracking and model registries solve, and they solve two different halves of it.

Experiment tracking logs every single training run automatically: the hyperparameters that went in, the metrics that came out, the code version that produced it, and the resulting artifact. A model registry is a separate, versioned catalog layered on top, holding only the models worth keeping, each one tagged with a promotion stage. Skip either one, and you can't answer 'reproduce this' or 'which model is live' with any confidence.

In practice, this is just a few lines wrapped around your training script. MLflow — the standard, open-source tool in this category — logs every parameter and metric to a tracking server as the run happens. Once that's done, 'show me every run where accuracy beat ninety-four percent' becomes a real query against permanent records instead of a memory someone has to dig up.

A registry adds versioning and status on top: fraud-model version one, two, three, each moving through stages — none, staging, production, archived. Promoting a version to production is a deliberate, logged action, not a quiet file copy nobody remembers making. And rolling back a bad promotion just means pointing the production alias back at the previous version, not hunting through backups.

This pair of practices is the foundation the rest of the chapter stands on. CI/CD for models needs the registry to know the current production version so a new candidate has something real to beat. Monitoring needs to know exactly which registered version is deployed so an alert points at the right model, not a guess.

With tracking and registries in place, every training run is reproducible and every deployed model is a known, versioned quantity. Next, lesson nineteen takes that foundation and builds automated retraining triggers and evaluation gates on top of it — CI/CD applied to models instead of application code.
